# 16.3 Observability dashboard and load-test report

← [16.2 Live deployment on Kubernetes with CI/CD; ADRs, runbook and architecture diagrams](../16.2-deployment-adrs-runbook/README.md) · [Module 16](../README.md) · [Phase 3](../../README.md) · [16.4 System-design interview practice](../16.4-system-design-interviews/README.md) →

> **Week 37** · Module 16: Capstone, System Design & Interview Prep · Website topic covered: *An observability dashboard and a load-test report with findings and fixes*

## What you will be able to do

- Turn the Module 13 dashboard into one that answers "are customers' transfers working?" in ten seconds.
- Plan a final load test of the deployed system: expected peak, twice the peak, and a soak.
- Change one thing at a time, and show each finding with evidence and before-and-after numbers.
- Write a load-test report that an engineering manager can read in five minutes and trust.
- Present the dashboard and the report in your defence and in interviews.

## Why this matters in a bank or fintech

"It works on my machine" isn't evidence, and neither is "it handled a lot of traffic". Before a launch, a bank wants to know what load the system was tested at, on what hardware, what broke first and what was done about it. A clear report with honest numbers is one of the strongest things you can show an employer: it proves you can measure, reason from evidence and write it down, which is most of what production support is.

## 1. The dashboard for `v1.0`

In Module 13 you built panels as you learned each signal. For `v1.0`, reorganise the dashboard around the questions people ask, top to bottom:

| Row | Question | Panels |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Customers | Are transfers working right now? | Transfer requests per second, error ratio, p95 latency against the SLO line, error budget remaining |
| 2. Money flow | Is money moving through every step? | Transfers by state (`REQUESTED`, `RESERVED`, `CLEARED`, `POSTED`, `FAILED`), saga duration p95, outbox oldest age, consumer lag per group, DLT messages |
| 3. Services | Which service is the problem? | RED metrics per service (rate, errors, duration), circuit-breaker state |
| 4. Saturation | What's running out? | CPU and memory against limits, JVM heap, database connections in use and waiting, Kafka consumer threads, pod count from the HPA |
| 5. Features | Are the extras healthy? | Cache hit ratio, rates stream subscribers, assistant tokens, latency and refusals |

The top row is what you look at when paged; the rows below are where you go next. Keep it in Git (provisioned from a file, as in topic 13.2), use the same time range and units on every panel, and draw the SLO as a line on the latency panel so "good" and "bad" are visible without reading numbers.

Link the dashboard to traces and logs: from a slow-request panel, an exemplar opens the trace in Tempo, and from the trace, the logs with the same trace id (topics 13.1 and 13.2). In the defence, that path from "the graph went up" to "this line of code" is what assessors want to see.

## 2. Planning the final load test

Run it on the **deployed** system, not on your laptop's Docker Compose, and write the plan down before you start:

| Item | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Question | Does `v1.0` meet the transfer SLOs at the expected salary-day peak, and what breaks first? |
| Environment | 3-node k3s cluster, 4 vCPU and 8 GB each; PostgreSQL on its own node; images `3f9c2a1b7d40` |
| Traffic model | 90% status polls, 10% new transfers; 1% of transfers above the fraud limit; arrival rate, not fixed users |
| Expected peak | 40 transfers a second (your own estimate, with the reasoning written down) |
| Runs | Baseline at the peak; twice the peak; a 30-minute soak at the peak |
| Pass | Error ratio < 1%, transfer creation p95 < 500 ms, outbox oldest age < 10 s, no restarts |
| Watching | The dashboard above, JFR on the slowest service, `kubectl top pods`, database slow-query log |

The **expected peak** must come from reasoning, not a round number: for example 200,000 active customers, 1.5 transfers each on salary day, half of them in the busiest two hours, gives about 21 transfers a second on average in those hours; double it for spikes within the hour, and 40 a second is a fair peak. Interviewers ask exactly this kind of estimate (topic 16.4).

The **soak test** runs at the peak for longer than feels useful. It finds what a five-minute test can't: memory that grows slowly, connection pools that leak, a log volume that fills a disk, a cache that never expires, the batch job starting at midnight in the middle of the run.

Load-test only systems you own, from a machine that can generate the load (k6 on a separate VM near the cluster, or k6 inside the cluster as a Job), and never against shared or third-party endpoints. Point the FX and SMS providers at your stubs.

## 3. Finding and fixing: one change at a time

The method is the one from topic 13.5, now on the real deployment:

1. **Run** the baseline and save the k6 summary, screenshots of the dashboard rows, and any traces of the slowest requests.
2. **Find the first bottleneck** with evidence: which SLO broke first, which panel moved first, what the profiler or the slow-query log says. Write down your hypothesis.
3. **Change one thing.** A pool size, an index, a lock, a batch size, a replica count, a resource limit. If you change two, you won't know which helped.
4. **Run the same test again** and compare the same numbers.
5. **Keep or revert** the change, and write it down either way. A change that didn't help is a finding too.

Typical first bottlenecks on a deployed ITL Pay, and the evidence that shows each:

| Symptom | Evidence | Usual fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Latency rises, CPU at its limit, pods not scaling | `kubectl top`, HPA status, throttling metric | Fix requests and limits, or the HPA target |
| Requests waiting for a database connection | Hikari "pending" panel | Shorter transactions first; then the pool size |
| One slow query at the top of the slow-query log | `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` | An index, or fewer queries (N+1) |
| Outbox age rising under load | Outbox panel, relay logs | Batch sends (13.5), more relay throughput |
| Consumer lag growing on one group | Lag panel per partition | More partitions and consumers, or a faster handler |
| Memory rising slowly in the soak | Heap after GC rising over 30 minutes | Heap dump and Eclipse MAT (13.3) |

## 4. The report

Write it for an engineering manager who has five minutes. One page of summary, then the evidence:

```markdown
# ITL Pay v1.0 load-test report

## Summary
At the expected peak (40 transfers/s) v1.0 meets both transfer SLOs. At twice the peak, transfer creation p95
rises to 820 ms (SLO 500 ms) because accounts' database connections are exhausted. A 30-minute soak at the peak
showed no memory growth and no errors. One fix made (shorter hold transaction), one planned (read replica for
status polls).

## Environment and method
<cluster, versions, image tags, traffic model, k6 script link, what was watched>

## Results
| Run | Rate | Requests | Errors | Create p95 | Status p95 | Outbox oldest | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Baseline | 40/s | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | |
| 2 Twice the peak | 80/s | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | connections exhausted |
| 3 After fix | 80/s | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | |
| 4 Soak, 30 min | 40/s | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | heap flat |

## Findings
1. <finding, evidence (graph, trace, profile), change, before and after>

## Limits and next steps
<what wasn't tested, known risks, what you'd do next>
```

The numbers in that summary are an example of the shape, not a target. What makes a report credible:

- **Percentiles, not averages**, and the error count alongside the latency.
- **The environment written down**: the same test on a laptop and on a cluster gives different numbers, and both are fine if labelled.
- **Every claim linked to evidence**: a graph, a trace, a profile, a query plan.
- **What you didn't test**: no second region, stubbed providers, synthetic data. Honesty here is what makes the rest believable.

Keep the report in the repository as `docs/load-test-v1.0.md`, with the k6 script and the raw summaries, so anyone can run it again.

## 5. Presenting it

In the defence and in interviews you'll have two minutes for this. Practise saying it in this order:

1. **The headline:** "At the expected peak of 40 transfers a second, both SLOs held; at twice the peak, creation latency broke the SLO."
2. **The bottleneck and the evidence:** "The Hikari panel showed requests waiting for connections in accounts; the traces showed the hold transaction staying open while it published a notification."
3. **The fix and the numbers:** "I moved the notification out of the transaction, after commit; the waits went from 25 to 2 and p95 dropped from 820 to 390 milliseconds."
4. **What's next:** "The next limit is the primary database; status polls could go to a read replica."

Have the dashboard open on the deployed system, not screenshots, and know where every panel's query comes from.

## Worked example: a soak-test finding

Chidi's baseline and twice-the-peak runs are clean, but in the 30-minute soak, transfers' heap after garbage collection climbs steadily from 210 MB to 470 MB, and the pod is restarted for exceeding its memory limit at minute 26. A five-minute run would never have shown it.

A heap histogram (topic 13.3) shows millions of entries in a `ConcurrentHashMap` inside his rate limiter: one entry per customer, never removed. He replaces it with a bounded cache with expiry, runs the same soak, and the heap stays between 200 and 230 MB for the full 30 minutes with no restarts. The finding goes into the report with both graphs, and into his STAR stories for topic 16.5.

## Common mistakes

- Load-testing Docker Compose on a laptop and reporting it as the deployed system's capacity.
- An "expected peak" with no reasoning behind it.
- Only short runs, so slow leaks and scheduled jobs never show up.
- Changing several settings between runs.
- A report full of graphs with no summary, or a summary with no evidence.
- Averages instead of percentiles; latency without errors; no environment.
- Load-testing a provider's sandbox or a shared environment you don't own.
- A dashboard nobody can read in ten seconds, with the most important panel at the bottom.

## Practice

1. Reorganise your dashboard into the five rows of section 1, with the SLO line on the latency panel, and keep it in Git.
2. Write your load-test plan, including the reasoning for your expected peak, and have your mentor review it.
3. Run the baseline, twice the peak and a 30-minute soak against your deployed system, saving the summaries and screenshots.
4. Make one change for the first bottleneck you find, rerun the same test, and record before and after.
5. Write `docs/load-test-v1.0.md` in the format of section 4.
6. Record yourself presenting the report in two minutes, and watch it back.
